emt-airway-l01.q: An adult has a tidal volume of 300 mL and a rate of 20. About how much air actually reaches the alveoli each minute?
emt-airway-l01.why: Dead space costs 150 mL of every breath, so only 150 mL of each 300 mL breath is useful. 150 x 20 = 3,000 mL. The 6,000 mL figure is the raw minute volume, which is the number that hides the problem.

emt-airway-l01.q: A drowning victim pulled from a pool is breathing 6 times a minute with barely visible chest rise and an SpO2 of 84%. Which step is primarily failing, and what fixes it?
choices: Respiration at the cell; give a nonrebreather
Ventilation; bag-valve mask with oxygen
Oxygenation only; nasal cannula at 6 L/min
Respiration at the cell; nothing an EMT carries will help
emt-airway-l01.why: A rate of 6 with poor depth is a mechanical failure to move air, which is ventilation. Only positive pressure fixes it. A nonrebreather or cannula enriches air the patient is not moving, so neither helps.

emt-airway-l02.q: A 4-year-old has aspirated a piece of hot dog. Which lung is it most likely to have entered, and why?
choices: Left, because the left bronchus is wider
Right, because the right mainstem bronchus leaves the carina at a straighter angle
Left, because the heart pushes objects leftward
Neither; objects lodge at the cricoid ring in children
emt-airway-l02.why: The right mainstem is straighter, so gravity and airflow carry material there. The left bronchus angles more sharply. The cricoid ring is the narrowest point in a child but it sits above the carina, and a hot dog piece small enough to pass the cords keeps going.

emt-airway-l02.q: Which structure is the only complete ring of cartilage in the entire airway?
choices: The thyroid cartilage
The first tracheal ring
The cricoid cartilage
The carina
emt-airway-l02.why: The cricoid is the one complete ring. The thyroid cartilage is open posteriorly, the tracheal rings are C-shaped, and the carina is a branch point, not a ring.

emt-airway-l03.q: An infant with pneumonia is grunting with every exhalation. What does grunting mean?
choices: Upper airway obstruction from the tongue
The infant is generating back-pressure to keep alveoli open, which is a red flag
Fluid in the large airways that will clear with suction
Normal infant breathing noise below 6 months
emt-airway-l03.why: Grunting is an infant's own version of PEEP, closing the glottis against exhalation to splint alveoli. It signals significant distress. Tongue obstruction produces snoring, and large-airway mucus produces rhonchi.

emt-airway-l03.q: Which set of findings best matches LATE hypoxia rather than early hypoxia?
choices: Anxiety, restlessness, tachycardia, pale sweaty skin
Sleepiness, confusion, bradycardia, central cyanosis
Slightly elevated blood pressure and a fast respiratory rate
Irritability with a normal SpO2
emt-airway-l03.why: Early hypoxia is a fight: anxious, fast, pale. Late hypoxia is surrender: sleepy, slow heart rate, falling pressure, blue. Cyanosis is a late sign, never an early one.

emt-airway-l04.q: You are about to suction an unresponsive adult. In what order do you set the catheter depth and turn on suction?
choices: Suction on, insert to the corner of the mouth to earlobe depth, suction while withdrawing
Measure corner of mouth to earlobe, insert with suction off, apply suction while withdrawing
Insert as deep as it will go with suction on, then withdraw slowly
Measure nostril to earlobe, insert with suction on, release on withdrawal
emt-airway-l04.why: Measure corner of mouth to earlobe, insert with suction off so you do not strip oxygen on the way in or grab mucosa, and suction on the way out. Nostril to earlobe is the NPA landmark, not the suction landmark.

emt-airway-l04.q: An unresponsive 6-month-old has formula in the mouth. What is your maximum suction time per attempt?
choices: 5 seconds
10 seconds
15 seconds
20 seconds
emt-airway-l04.why: Infant 5 seconds, child 10 seconds, adult 15 seconds. Infants have the smallest oxygen reserve and the strongest vagal response to pharyngeal stimulation, so they get the shortest window.

emt-airway-l05.q: An OPA that is measured too LONG causes which specific problem?
choices: It pushes the tongue backward into the pharynx
It can press the epiglottis down over the laryngeal opening
It cannot be secured and falls out
It blocks the nasal passage
emt-airway-l05.why: Too long reaches past the tongue and can fold the epiglottis over the airway. Too SHORT is what pushes the tongue backward. Both errors obstruct, but by different mechanisms, and the exam tests which is which.

emt-airway-l05.q: You are lubricating an NPA before insertion. Which lubricant and which bevel orientation are correct?
choices: Petroleum jelly, bevel away from the septum
Water-soluble jelly, bevel toward the septum
Petroleum jelly, bevel toward the septum
No lubricant, bevel away from the septum
emt-airway-l05.why: Water-soluble jelly only; petroleum products are not absorbed and can cause lipoid pneumonia if aspirated. The bevel faces the septum so the tip slides along the flat wall instead of catching on turbinates.

emt-airway-l06.q: A patient on a nasal cannula at 6 L/min still has an SpO2 of 88% with good chest rise and full sentences. What is the correct change?
choices: Increase the cannula to 10 L/min
Switch to a nonrebreather at 10-15 L/min
Begin bag-valve mask ventilation
Add humidification and keep the cannula at 6 L/min
emt-airway-l06.why: Above 6 L/min a cannula dries the nose without delivering meaningfully more, so cranking it is the classic error. The patient is moving air adequately, so a bag is not indicated; step up the device instead.

emt-airway-l06.q: Roughly what delivered oxygen concentration does a nasal cannula at 3 L/min provide?
choices: About 21%
About 32%
About 44%
About 60%
emt-airway-l06.why: Each liter adds roughly 4% over room air's 21%, so 3 L/min gives about 33%. 21% is room air with no flow, 44% is 6 L/min, and 60% is the top of the simple face mask range.

emt-airway-l07.q: A D cylinder reads 2,000 psi and you plan to run a nonrebreather at 15 L/min for a 25-minute transport. Will it last?
choices: Yes, about 33 minutes
No, about 19 minutes
Yes, about 21 minutes
No, about 12 minutes
emt-airway-l07.why: (2000 - 200) x 0.16 = 288, divided by 15 = about 19 minutes. It will not cover the transport. The 33-minute answer uses the E constant of 0.28, which is the second most common exam mistake after forgetting to subtract 200.

emt-airway-l07.q: How often must a medical oxygen cylinder be hydrostatically tested, and where is the date found?
choices: Every 5 years, stamped on the cylinder shoulder
Every year, printed on the regulator
Every 10 years, on the pin-index yoke
Every 5 years, on the gasket
emt-airway-l07.why: Hydrostatic testing is every 5 years and the date is stamped into the metal at the shoulder. Regulators, yokes and gaskets are not where the cylinder's test date lives.

emt-airway-l08.q: You are bagging an apneic adult with a pulse and counting out loud. Which count matches the correct rate?
choices: Squeeze on every count of 3
Squeeze on every count of 6
Squeeze on every count of 2
Squeeze on every count of 10
emt-airway-l08.why: An adult with a pulse gets 1 breath every 6 seconds, 10 per minute. Every 2-3 seconds is the pediatric rate. Every 10 seconds is too slow to maintain minute volume.

emt-airway-l08.q: Your partner asks whether to apply cricoid pressure during bag-valve mask ventilation. The correct answer is:
choices: Yes, it reliably prevents aspiration
Yes, but only in children
No, it is no longer routinely recommended and can deform the airway
No, because it is a paramedic-only skill
emt-airway-l08.why: Cricoid pressure (Sellick) was dropped because it does not reliably prevent aspiration and it can compress and obstruct the airway. It is not a scope issue; it is an effectiveness issue.

emt-airway-l09.q: Why does CPAP help a pulmonary edema patient beyond simply adding oxygen?
choices: It dries secretions in the large airways
It pushes alveolar fluid back into the capillaries and reduces preload and afterload
It delivers a measured tidal volume with each breath
It blocks the esophagus and prevents vomiting
emt-airway-l09.why: Constant pressure recruits alveoli, drives edema fluid back across the membrane, and unloads the left ventricle by dropping preload and afterload. CPAP delivers no set tidal volume, that is a ventilator, and it does nothing to the esophagus.

emt-airway-l09.q: A COPD patient in distress has a systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg. CPAP is:
choices: Indicated, because CPAP raises blood pressure
Contraindicated, because raised intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return
Indicated at 5 cmH2O only
Contraindicated only if the patient is also vomiting
emt-airway-l09.why: Hypotension, generally systolic under 90, is a contraindication: positive pressure in the chest squeezes venous return and can drop the pressure further. Lowering the setting does not remove the problem.

emt-airway-l10.q: A visibly pregnant woman at a restaurant cannot speak, is making no sound, and is clutching her throat. What do you deliver?
choices: Abdominal thrusts just above the navel
Chest thrusts at the mid-sternum
Back slaps only
A blind finger sweep, then abdominal thrusts
emt-airway-l10.why: Late pregnancy and patients too large to reach around get chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. Back slaps alone are the infant sequence, and blind finger sweeps are never correct at any age.

emt-airway-l10.q: A paramedic asks you to preoxygenate before an intubation attempt. For how long, at minimum?
choices: 10 seconds
30 seconds
3 minutes
Only until the SpO2 reads 90%
emt-airway-l10.why: At least 30 seconds of preoxygenation builds reserve before the attempt. Ten seconds is too short to make a difference, and waiting for only 90% leaves the patient starting the attempt already hypoxic.

emt-airway-l11.q: Your CPAP mask is leaking at the bridge of the nose. Which correction is correct?
choices: Tighten the straps until the leak stops completely
Reseat the mask higher and pull the bottom strap first, leaving well-fitting dentures in
Remove the patient's dentures to get a flatter surface
Raise the pressure from 5 to 10 cmH2O to overcome the leak
emt-airway-l11.why: Overtightening deforms the cushion and worsens the leak. Dentures give the face structure and should stay in. Raising the pressure does not fix a mechanical leak, it just blows harder through it.

emt-airway-l11.q: A full D cylinder is driving a CPAP circuit consuming 30 L/min. About how long do you have?
choices: Under 10 minutes
About 17 minutes
About 25 minutes
About 34 minutes
emt-airway-l11.why: (2000 - 200) x 0.16 = 288, divided by 30 = about 9.6 minutes. The 17-minute answer is the same math on an E cylinder. This is why you move to the onboard M cylinder as soon as you are in the truck.

emt-airway-l12.q: A ventilator alarms for LOW pressure and low volume. Which cause fits best?
choices: The patient is biting the tube
A mucus plug in the tube
A disconnected circuit or a leaking tube cuff
A developing pneumothorax
emt-airway-l12.why: Low pressure means air is escaping: disconnection, loose fitting, cuff leak. Biting, plugs and pneumothorax all increase resistance and set off the HIGH pressure alarm instead.

emt-airway-l12.q: A patient on a home ventilator deteriorates and you cannot fix it in seconds. What is the one rule that always works?
choices: Increase the FiO2 on the machine to 1.00
Disconnect from the machine and bag by hand at 15 L/min, then run DOPE
Silence the alarm and transport rapidly
Raise the PEEP setting to 10 cmH2O
emt-airway-l12.why: Taking them off the machine and squeezing a bag tells you in one squeeze whether the problem is obstruction, leak or chest. Adjusting settings on a machine you did not set wastes the minute you have.

emt-airway-l13.q: You are choosing an i-gel for a patient who weighs about 55 kg. Which size and what do you do with the cuff?
choices: Size 3, inflate with 45-60 mL
Size 4, inflate with 60-80 mL
Size 3 or 4, and there is no cuff to inflate
Size 5, no cuff to inflate
emt-airway-l13.why: 55 kg falls in the overlap of size 3 (30-60 kg) and size 4 (50-90 kg). The i-gel has no inflatable cuff at all; it is a thermoplastic gel cradle. Cuff volumes belong to the King LT.

emt-airway-l13.q: Which finding absolutely rules out placing a supraglottic airway?
choices: An SpO2 of 78%
An intact gag reflex
A heart rate of 42
Facial bruising
emt-airway-l13.why: An intact gag reflex is the absolute contraindication; the device will trigger vomiting. Severe hypoxia and bradycardia are reasons to manage the airway, not reasons to avoid it, and facial bruising does not block an oral device.

emt-airway-l14.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is breathing deeply at 32 and has clear lungs. What ETCO2 do you expect, and why?
choices: Above 50 mmHg, because the rate is high
Under 25 mmHg, because deep rapid breathing is blowing off CO2
Normal at 35-45 mmHg, because the lungs are clear
No waveform, because deep breathing outruns the sensor
emt-airway-l14.why: Kussmaul breathing is the body deliberately blowing off CO2 to compensate for acidosis, so ETCO2 falls below 25. Above 50 is hypoventilation, the opposite picture. Clear lungs do not guarantee a normal number.

emt-airway-l14.q: Why does capnography detect apnea during procedural sedation before the pulse oximeter does?
choices: The oximeter samples more slowly than the capnograph
A preoxygenated patient's saturation stays near 100% for 30-60 seconds after breathing stops, while the waveform flattens immediately
Capnography measures oxygen directly
The oximeter only works on a finger
emt-airway-l14.why: Saturation lags because the patient has a lungful of oxygen already loaded on hemoglobin. The CO2 waveform depends on air actually leaving the lungs, so it disappears the moment ventilation stops.

emt-airway-l15.q: A trach patient's tube came out entirely 3 days after surgery. What do you do?
choices: Force the spare tube back into the stoma immediately
Cover the stoma and bag from the face if the upper airway is intact, and transport
Insert the obturator alone into the stoma
Suction the stoma deeply to reopen the tract
emt-airway-l15.why: A stoma less than about a week old has an immature tract, and forcing a tube can place it into neck tissue instead of the trachea. If the upper airway is connected, cover the stoma and ventilate from the face. The obturator is a guide, not an airway.

emt-airway-l15.q: In the DOPE check, which problem does removing the inner cannula address?
choices: Displacement
Obstruction
Pneumothorax
Equipment
emt-airway-l15.why: The inner cannula is the part that plugs with mucus, so pulling and inspecting it is the fastest obstruction check. Displacement is checked by depth, sounds and waveform; equipment is checked by bagging off the machine.

emt-airway-l16.q: A firefighter is unconscious after an enclosed-space fire, has an SpO2 of 98%, no burns, and is severely acidotic. What should you suspect and what is your job?
choices: Simple smoke irritation; observe
Cyanide toxicity from burning plastics; give high-flow oxygen and move fast toward the ALS antidote
Carbon monoxide only; a normal SpO2 rules out cyanide
Head injury; withhold oxygen until imaging
emt-airway-l16.why: Burning plastics and foam release cyanide, which poisons the cell's use of oxygen, so oxygenation looks perfect while the patient dies. Hydroxocobalamin is an ALS drug; oxygen and speed are yours. A normal SpO2 rules out nothing in a fire.

emt-airway-l16.q: You are ventilating a woman who is 30 weeks pregnant. Beyond ramping, what positioning change matters?
choices: Tilt her 15-30 degrees to the left to take the uterus off the vena cava
Keep her flat and supine to protect the spine
Tilt her 15-30 degrees to the right
Raise the legs 12 inches
emt-airway-l16.why: Past about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when supine, cutting venous return. Left tilt relieves it. Right tilt does nothing helpful, and raising the legs does not move the uterus off the vessel.

emt-airway-l17.q: A stroke patient is alert with an SpO2 of 96% on room air. What oxygen is indicated?
choices: Nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min
None; give oxygen only if the SpO2 falls below 94%
CPAP at 5 cmH2O
emt-airway-l17.why: Stroke guidance is to give oxygen only below 94%. Routine oxygen in a well-saturated stroke patient adds vasoconstriction without benefit. CPAP has no role in an alert stroke patient breathing adequately.

emt-airway-l17.q: Why does giving oxygen to a well-saturated heart attack patient potentially cause harm?
choices: It raises carbon dioxide dangerously
It constricts coronary vessels, slightly reducing flow to the threatened muscle
It causes immediate absorption atelectasis within seconds
It falsely lowers the SpO2 reading
emt-airway-l17.why: Hyperoxia causes coronary and cerebral vasoconstriction, which is why oxygen is withheld at an SpO2 of 90% or above in chest pain. Absorption atelectasis is real but develops over a longer period, not seconds.

emt-airway-l18.q: Two rescuers are working a pediatric arrest with no advanced airway. What is the compression-to-ventilation ratio?
choices: Continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds
emt-airway-l18.why: Two-rescuer pediatric CPR is 15:2 because children arrest from hypoxia and need more ventilation. 30:2 is the adult ratio and the single-rescuer pediatric ratio. Continuous compressions with a breath every 6 seconds requires an advanced airway.

emt-airway-l18.q: Immediately after ROSC, which combination is correct?
choices: 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 100%, head flat
10 breaths per minute, ETCO2 35-45, SpO2 titrated to 92-98%
10 breaths per minute, SpO2 100% maintained, aggressive rewarming
30 breaths per minute, ETCO2 under 25, head elevated
emt-airway-l18.why: Post-ROSC is 10 per minute targeting an ETCO2 of 35-45 with oxygen titrated to 92-98% and the head up about 30 degrees. Fast bagging drops CO2 and constricts cerebral vessels; sustained 100% oxygen and aggressive rewarming are both harms.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old with a chest wall injury is breathing 28 times a minute with a tidal volume you estimate at 200 mL. His partner in the same crash breathes 14 times a minute at 450 mL. Which statement is correct?
choices: The first patient is moving substantially less alveolar air because dead space eats most of each small breath
The first patient is compensating adequately because his rate is higher
The second patient is hypoventilating because his rate is below 20
Both are moving about the same useful air because their minute volumes are similar
quiz.why: Dead space costs a fixed 150 mL per breath. Patient one delivers 50 mL x 28 = 1,400 mL to the alveoli; patient two delivers 300 mL x 14 = 4,200 mL. The raw minute volumes look similar, which is exactly the trap. A rate of 14 is normal, not hypoventilation.

quiz.q: A patient with severe pulmonary edema has excellent chest rise at a rate of 24 but an SpO2 of 80% on a nonrebreather. Which process is primarily failing?
choices: Ventilation
Oxygenation
Respiration at the cell
All three equally
quiz.why: Air is moving well, so ventilation is intact. Fluid between the alveolus and the capillary is blocking oxygen from crossing, which is an oxygenation failure. Cellular respiration failure is the cyanide picture, where saturation looks normal.

quiz.q: A 72-year-old with known COPD has an SpO2 of 86%. You place oxygen and the saturation climbs to 97%. Ten minutes later he is drowsy and his respiratory rate has fallen to 8. The best action is to:
choices: Apply CPAP at 10 cmH2O
Remove all oxygen immediately
Titrate the oxygen down toward 88-92% and begin assisting ventilations with a bag-valve mask
Increase the oxygen to 15 L/min by nonrebreather
quiz.why: The target was overshot and CO2 has climbed, so titrate down and support the inadequate rate with positive pressure. Removing oxygen entirely re-creates the hypoxia that kills faster. CPAP requires a patient who is awake and able to follow commands, which this one no longer is.

quiz.q: You are ventilating a 5-year-old and want a neutral airway position. Where does the padding go?
choices: Under the hips, to open the chest
No padding is needed at any age
Under the head, because the occiput is small
Under the shoulders, because the large occiput flexes the neck when supine
quiz.why: A child's large occiput pushes the head forward and kinks the airway when lying flat, so padding goes under the shoulders. Padding under the head worsens the flexion. Adults are the ones who sometimes need occipital padding to reach the sniffing position.

quiz.q: A 4-month-old has thick nasal congestion, is feeding poorly, and has mild retractions. Why is this an airway concern rather than a simple cold?
choices: Infants under about 6 months breathe almost entirely through the nose
Infants have a narrower trachea than the nose
Infants cannot cough
The epiglottis blocks the mouth in infants
quiz.why: Obligate nasal breathing until about 6 months makes a blocked nose a real airway obstruction, and suctioning it is a genuine intervention. Infants can cough, and the epiglottis does not block the mouth.

quiz.q: Which statement about the narrowest point of the airway is correct?
choices: It is the cricoid ring at every age
It is the vocal cords in adults and the cricoid ring in children under about 8-10
It is the vocal cords at every age
It is the carina in children and the cords in adults
quiz.why: Adults narrow at the cords; children narrow at the cricoid ring until roughly age 8-10. This matters because a tube that passes a child's cords can still be too big below them. The carina is a branch point, not a narrowing.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with a barking cough has high-pitched noise on inspiration that you can hear across the room. This sound and its origin are:
choices: Crackles from fluid in the alveoli
Wheezing from the bronchioles
Stridor from narrowing above the vocal cords
Rhonchi from mucus in the large airways
quiz.why: Stridor is an upper airway sound from narrowing above the cords, classic in croup. Wheezes come from constricted bronchioles below the cords, rhonchi from secretions, crackles from alveolar fluid. Mislabeling stridor as wheezing leads to the wrong treatment.

quiz.q: Which single finding is the most reliable early sign of respiratory distress in a child?
choices: A respiratory rate of 26
An SpO2 of 93%
Cyanosis of the lips
Retractions of the skin between the ribs and above the collarbones
quiz.why: Retractions show increased work of breathing before any number moves, and they are the most reliable pediatric sign. Cyanosis is late. A rate of 26 is within normal for a child, and 93% is only marginally low.

quiz.q: An 8-month-old infant at rest has a respiratory rate of 22. This rate is:
choices: Below normal and concerning
Above normal and concerning
Normal only if the infant is asleep
Normal for this age
quiz.why: Normal infant rate under 1 year is 25-50. A rate of 22 in an infant is slow and suggests fatigue or impending failure. The same number in an adult would be mildly fast, which is why age-specific ranges matter.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient found face-down in a driveway with an unwitnessed mechanism has snoring respirations. Your first airway maneuver is:
choices: Head-tilt chin-lift
Jaw thrust with in-line stabilization
Insert a nasopharyngeal airway
Place in the recovery position
quiz.why: An unwitnessed unresponsive trauma patient gets a jaw thrust first because a spine injury is possible. If the jaw thrust fails, you go to head-tilt chin-lift anyway, because a patent airway outranks a theoretical spine injury. An adjunct comes after the airway is opened.

quiz.q: Which suction tip is correct for clearing thick vomit from the mouth of an unresponsive adult, and why?
choices: Either one, because bore size does not affect clearance
Soft French catheter, because it is atraumatic
Rigid Yankauer, because its large bore handles thick material and you can see where it goes
Soft French catheter, because it reaches deeper
quiz.why: The rigid tip is the workhorse for the mouth: big bore for chunks and blood, used only where you can see. The soft catheter clogs on anything thick and belongs in the nose, an NPA, a trach or an ET tube.

quiz.q: You clamp the suction tubing to test the unit before a call. What minimum vacuum should it generate?
choices: 500 mmHg
100 mmHg
200 mmHg
300 mmHg
quiz.why: A functioning unit should pull at least 300 mmHg when the tubing is clamped. Lower readings mean the unit will not move thick material. 200 mmHg is the safe residual pressure for an oxygen cylinder, which is a different number entirely.

quiz.q: You insert an OPA in an unresponsive adult by rotating it 180 degrees. Afterward the patient's breathing sounds more obstructed than before. The most likely explanation is:
choices: The airway was too short and pushed the tongue backward
The airway was correctly sized but needs suction
The rotation technique is wrong in adults
The patient needs a larger nasal airway instead
quiz.why: A too-short OPA acts like a tongue depressor pushing the tongue back into the pharynx. The 180-degree rotation is correct for adults; it is children who must never be rotated. Remeasure corner of mouth to earlobe and resize.

quiz.q: A postictal patient has clenched teeth, snoring respirations, and an intact gag reflex. There is no facial trauma. The correct adjunct is:
choices: Oropharyngeal airway, inserted sideways
Nasopharyngeal airway
No adjunct; position only
Supraglottic airway
quiz.why: An NPA is tolerated with a gag reflex and passes around clenched teeth, making it the adjunct for postictal and semi-conscious overdose patients. An OPA is contraindicated with a gag, and a supraglottic airway requires an absent gag.

quiz.q: You insert a nasopharyngeal airway and the patient's nose bleeds a small amount. The airway is seated and the patient's breathing has improved. You should:
choices: Remove it and insert a larger NPA in the other nostril
Remove the NPA immediately and pack the nostril
Leave the NPA in place, keep suction ready, and monitor
Remove it and place an OPA instead
quiz.why: Minor bleeding after NPA insertion is common and is usually not a reason to remove it. Pulling it out leaves you with both an obstructed airway and a bleeding nose. An OPA is not an option in a patient with a gag reflex.

quiz.q: A patient needs 60% oxygen but cannot tolerate a nonrebreather because of claustrophobia. He is alert with good chest rise. Which device is the best compromise?
choices: Bag-valve mask held loosely over the face
Blow-by at 6 L/min
Nasal cannula at 10 L/min
Simple face mask at 10 L/min
quiz.why: A simple mask at 6-10 L/min delivers 35-60% and is a legitimate middle step. A cannula above 6 L/min just dries the nose. A bag-valve mask is a ventilation device, not a comfort measure, and blow-by is a pediatric technique delivering far less.

quiz.q: Before placing a nonrebreather on a patient's face you should:
choices: Cover the valve and prime the reservoir bag until it fills
Remove the one-way valves so the patient can exhale
Attach humidification for all patients
Run it at 6 L/min to conserve oxygen
quiz.why: Priming fills the reservoir so the first breath delivers high concentration. Running at 6 L/min is too low for a nonrebreather, which needs 10-15. The one-way valves are what make it a nonrebreather, and humidification is for long transports or dry-airway complaints.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old with an SpO2 of 90% screams and thrashes every time you bring a pediatric mask near her face. The best approach is:
choices: Restrain her head and hold the mask on
Have the parent hold oxygen tubing a few inches from her face at about 6 L/min
Withhold oxygen until she calms down on her own
Place a nasal cannula at 10 L/min
quiz.why: Blow-by at about 6 L/min held by a parent is a legitimate technique, not a consolation prize, because a screaming child consumes more oxygen than the mask would deliver. Forcing a mask makes the distress worse, and a cannula above 6 L/min is simply the wrong setting.

quiz.q: An M cylinder reads 1,000 psi. You are running 10 L/min. About how many minutes remain before safe residual?
choices: About 22 minutes
About 62 minutes
About 125 minutes
About 156 minutes
quiz.why: (1000 - 200) x 1.56 = 1,248, divided by 10 = about 125 minutes. The 156-minute answer forgets to subtract the 200 psi residual. The 22-minute answer uses the E constant.

quiz.q: Which practice regarding an oxygen cylinder valve is correct?
choices: Crack it open sharply to clear debris while the regulator is attached
Leave it closed and rely on the regulator to open the flow
Open it a quarter turn only, to limit flow
Open it fully, then back it off a quarter turn
quiz.why: Open fully so flow is unrestricted, then back off a quarter turn so the next person can tell it is open rather than jammed shut. Opening only a quarter turn restricts flow at high liter settings, and the regulator does not open the cylinder valve.

quiz.q: A regulator will not seal against the cylinder and hisses. The correct action is:
choices: Shut the valve, replace the gasket, and confirm the correct pin-index fitting
Apply a small amount of petroleum jelly to the gasket
Add a second washer to build up the seal
Tighten the yoke with a wrench until the hiss stops
quiz.why: Stacking washers and over-torquing both damage the fitting and can allow a high-pressure failure. Petroleum products near oxygen under pressure can ignite without a spark. Shut it down, fresh gasket, correct fitting.

quiz.q: You are alone ventilating an apneic adult and the chest rise is marginal. Your partner becomes free. The single best change is:
choices: Switch to a larger adult bag
Move to two-rescuer technique with a C-E grip on each side while your partner squeezes
Squeeze the bag harder and faster
Switch to a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
quiz.why: Two-rescuer bagging produces measurably higher tidal volumes because both hands hold the seal. Bag size is not the limiting factor; the seal is. Squeezing harder and faster causes gastric inflation and drops cardiac output, and a nonrebreather does not ventilate at all.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old is apneic with a palpable pulse of 110. You should ventilate:
choices: Once every 10 seconds
Once every 6 seconds
Once every 2-3 seconds
30 compressions to 2 breaths
quiz.why: A child or infant with a pulse gets 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, which is 20-30 per minute. Every 6 seconds is the adult rate and would badly underventilate this child. A pulse of 110 means this is not CPR.

quiz.q: You are bagging through a tracheostomy tube and air is escaping from the patient's mouth and nose. The correct action is:
choices: Stop and ventilate from the face instead
Deflate the trach cuff
Increase the rate to 20 per minute
Seal the mouth and nose and continue ventilating through the stoma
quiz.why: Air escaping upward means the upper airway is still connected, so sealing the mouth and nose directs your volume into the lungs. Ventilating from the face wastes the direct route you already have, and deflating the cuff would worsen the leak.

quiz.q: A 66-year-old with COPD is on CPAP at 7 cmH2O. After 8 minutes his respiratory rate has fallen from 34 to 24, he can say short sentences, and his SpO2 is 93%. His blood pressure is 138/84. You should:
choices: Continue CPAP and recheck the blood pressure every 5 minutes
Increase the pressure to 15 cmH2O
Switch to a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Remove CPAP because he has improved
quiz.why: This is exactly what success looks like within 5-10 minutes, so continue and keep cycling blood pressures every 5 minutes. Removing CPAP when it is working commonly causes an immediate relapse. EMT-level CPAP is generally capped at 5-10 cmH2O.

quiz.q: Which patient may receive CPAP?
choices: A 60-year-old with agonal respirations and an SpO2 of 70%
An awake 58-year-old with pneumonia, a rate of 28, SpO2 of 89%, and a blood pressure of 128/76
A 44-year-old with a stab wound to the chest and decreased breath sounds on the left
A 70-year-old vomiting repeatedly with an altered mental status
quiz.why: CPAP requires an awake, spontaneously breathing patient who can follow commands, and pneumonia with hypoxia is a supported indication. Agonal breathing needs a bag. Penetrating chest trauma and active vomiting are both contraindications.

quiz.q: A choking 6-year-old is coughing forcefully, wheezing between coughs, and is pink. You should:
choices: Deliver five back slaps and five chest thrusts
Begin abdominal thrusts immediately
Encourage coughing, give oxygen, stay close and transport
Perform a finger sweep to look for the object
quiz.why: A forceful cough moves more air than anything you can do by hand, so a mild obstruction is left alone. Intervening can convert it to a complete obstruction. Back slaps and chest thrusts are the infant sequence, and blind finger sweeps are never correct.

quiz.q: An adult choking victim who was receiving abdominal thrusts suddenly goes limp and slides to the floor. Your next action is:
choices: Insert an OPA and ventilate immediately
Continue abdominal thrusts on the ground
Perform a blind finger sweep, then ventilate
Begin CPR starting with chest compressions
quiz.why: Any choking patient who becomes unresponsive gets CPR beginning with compressions, because compressions generate airway pressure that can dislodge the object. You look in the mouth each time you open the airway to give a breath, but you never sweep blindly.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old has well-fitting dentures and needs bag-valve mask ventilation. You should:
choices: Leave the dentures in place to maintain facial structure and mask seal
Remove only the upper plate
Remove the dentures and insert an NPA instead
Remove the dentures to prevent aspiration
quiz.why: Well-fitting dentures give the face the structure your mask seals against. Remove only loose partials or broken plates that could become an obstruction. Taking out intact dentures makes the seal worse, not safer.

quiz.q: You are coaching a frightened patient onto CPAP. Which sequence is correct?
choices: Strap the mask on quickly, then explain what it feels like
Hold the mask against the face by hand, narrate what is coming, then strap it only until the leak stops
Start at 10 cmH2O so the benefit is immediate, then coach
Have the patient hold the mask themselves for the entire transport
quiz.why: Holding and narrating first lets the patient feel the flow before losing control of the mask, which is what prevents panic. Strapping first is the most common reason a patient rips it off. Pressure is started low and titrated up.

quiz.q: Your CPAP patient has a heavy beard and the mask leaks no matter how you seat it. The best response is:
choices: Shave the patient's face en route
Tighten the straps until the leak stops
Accept a partial benefit, watch the patient rather than the number, and be ready to bag
Abandon CPAP immediately and use a nonrebreather
quiz.why: A beard leaks and no amount of strap tension fixes it without deforming the cushion and worsening the seal. Partial pressure is still useful, so continue while watching work of breathing and mental status. Abandoning a working intervention outright gives up benefit you still have.

quiz.q: A CPAP patient's numbers look identical to when you started, but you notice the separate PEEP valve reads 2.5 cmH2O. You should:
choices: Remove CPAP and bag the patient
Increase the oxygen flow to 40 L/min
Leave it, since the patient tolerates it
Confirm and correct the valve setting to the intended pressure, then reassess
quiz.why: A PEEP valve knocked out of position in the bag looks identical to a correctly set one and delivers almost no therapy. Check the setting before concluding CPAP has failed. Bagging is for a deteriorating patient, not an untreated one.

quiz.q: A COPD patient is drowsy from carbon dioxide retention but still breathing on his own with a rate of 24. Which non-invasive support best matches the problem?
choices: BiPAP, because pressure support moves volume and clears CO2
A nonrebreather at 15 L/min
A nasal cannula at 6 L/min
CPAP, because it recruits alveoli
quiz.why: The problem is ventilation, not just oxygenation, so the patient needs the inspiratory boost that BiPAP's IPAP-EPAP difference provides. CPAP holds one pressure and mainly fixes oxygenation. Oxygen devices do not move volume at all.

quiz.q: Typical adult transport ventilator settings include a tidal volume of:
choices: 3-4 mL/kg ideal body weight
6-8 mL/kg ideal body weight
10-12 mL/kg actual body weight
15 mL/kg actual body weight
quiz.why: Current practice is 6-8 mL/kg of ideal body weight, which protects the lung from volume injury. Larger volumes and the use of actual rather than ideal weight both overdistend alveoli, especially in obese patients.

quiz.q: You disconnect a deteriorating ventilated patient and bag by hand. The bag is easy to squeeze but the chest does not rise. This suggests:
choices: Severe bronchospasm
A mucus plug in the tube
A leak or a displaced tube
A tension pneumothorax
quiz.why: Easy to squeeze with no chest rise means the air is going somewhere other than the lungs: a leak, a disconnected fitting, or a tube no longer in the trachea. Plugs, pneumothorax and bronchospasm all make the bag HARD to squeeze.

quiz.q: You are preparing an i-gel for a 110 kg adult in cardiac arrest. The correct size is:
choices: Size is chosen by height, not weight
quiz.why: i-gel sizing is by weight: 3 for 30-60 kg, 4 for 50-90 kg, 5 for over 90 kg. Height-based sizing belongs to the King LT. Choosing too small leaks and prevents you from generating volume.

quiz.q: A supraglottic airway is in place and ventilating well on scene. After moving the patient to the stretcher the chest rise disappears and the waveform is gone. Your first action is:
choices: Reassess the device position, reconfirm with breath sounds and waveform, and correct or remove it
Add more air to the cuff and continue
Assume the sensor failed and continue bagging
Increase the ventilation rate
quiz.why: These devices displace during every move, so loss of waveform after a move is a displaced airway until proven otherwise. Adding cuff volume to a malpositioned device can worsen it, and blaming the sensor is the error the exam is testing.

quiz.q: Which additional condition, beyond an intact gag reflex, contraindicates a supraglottic airway?
choices: A history of asthma
Known esophageal varices
Age over 65
An SpO2 below 80%
quiz.why: Known esophageal disease such as varices, caustic ingestion, and a foreign-body obstruction all rule the device out. Age, low saturation and asthma are not contraindications; severe hypoxia is a reason to secure the airway, not avoid it.

quiz.q: A patient with a suspected massive pulmonary embolism is breathing 30 times a minute with clear lungs and an ETCO2 of 18 mmHg. The low reading is best explained by:
choices: Hypoventilation from opioid effect
Airway obstruction preventing exhalation
Failure of circulation to deliver carbon dioxide to the lungs
A sensor reading room air
quiz.why: A clot blocks pulmonary blood flow, so CO2 never reaches the alveoli to be exhaled, and ETCO2 drops despite good air movement. Obstruction and hypoventilation raise ETCO2. A room-air sensor would show no waveform at all.

quiz.q: An opioid overdose patient on a nonrebreather has an SpO2 of 99% and an ETCO2 of 62 mmHg with a drowsy appearance. The correct interpretation is:
choices: The capnograph is malfunctioning
He is hyperventilating from anxiety
He is well oxygenated and stable
He is hypoventilating and needs assisted ventilation despite the saturation
quiz.why: An ETCO2 above 50 with a drowsy patient is hypoventilation, and it is the earliest warning you get. High-flow oxygen keeps the saturation high long after ventilation has failed, which is exactly the trap. Hyperventilation would drive ETCO2 down, not up.

quiz.q: After 20 minutes of good-quality resuscitation with an advanced airway, the ETCO2 remains at 6 mmHg. This finding is best used to:
choices: Inform a discussion about termination of resuscitation, as survival is very unlikely
Justify increasing the ventilation rate
Prove the capnograph has failed
Confirm the tube is in the esophagus
quiz.why: A persistent ETCO2 under 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of good CPR is associated with almost no chance of survival and is used in termination decisions. An esophageal tube shows no waveform at all, and raising the ventilation rate would lower ETCO2 further while harming cardiac output.

quiz.q: Which part of a tracheostomy tube should you remove and inspect first when a trach patient becomes short of breath?
choices: The obturator
The inner cannula
The outer cannula
The pilot balloon
quiz.why: The inner cannula is the removable liner that plugs with mucus, and pulling it is the single most useful first move. The obturator is only a guide for inserting a new tube. Removing the outer cannula pulls the airway out of the neck.

quiz.q: You have removed and cleared the inner cannula and suctioned a cuffed trach tube, but ventilation is still difficult. Your next step is:
choices: Increase the ventilation rate to 20 per minute
Force a new tube of the same size into the stoma
Deflate the cuff, since a herniated cuff can block the tube opening
Remove the outer cannula and ventilate the bare stoma
quiz.why: A cuff that has herniated over the distal opening blocks the tube from inside, and deflating it costs nothing to try. Forcing a new tube risks a false passage. Raising the rate does not overcome an obstruction.

quiz.q: How deep should a soft suction catheter be advanced into a tracheostomy tube?
choices: Corner of the mouth to the earlobe
Only to the hub, with continuous suction applied throughout
As far as it will go until resistance is felt
The length of the tube plus about 1-2 cm, suctioning only on withdrawal, 10 seconds maximum
quiz.why: Measured depth prevents trauma to the carina and the airway wall, suction is applied only on the way out, and 10 seconds is the limit with oxygenation between attempts. Corner of mouth to earlobe is the oral landmark, not the trach one.

quiz.q: A patient with facial burns and singed nasal hairs is currently speaking clearly with an SpO2 of 97%. The most important reason to transport promptly is:
choices: Airway swelling builds over minutes to hours and can close the airway en route
Burn pain will become unmanageable
He will develop pneumonia within the hour
The saturation will drop suddenly with no warning
quiz.why: Inhalation injury swelling is progressive, so the patient who looks fine at the curb can be unable to breathe later. The saturation is not the alarm here, and it can read falsely high with carbon monoxide. Pneumonia is a later complication, not the reason for speed.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old weighing 30 kg has hives, stridor and a swollen tongue after eating peanuts. The correct epinephrine dose and route is:
choices: 0.3 mg of 1 mg/mL IM in the lateral thigh
0.15 mg of 1 mg/mL IM in the lateral thigh
0.3 mg of 1 mg/mL subcutaneously in the upper arm
0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL IM in the deltoid
quiz.why: Pediatric anaphylaxis dosing is 0.15 mg IM in the lateral thigh, repeated in 5-15 minutes if needed; 0.3 mg is the adult dose. The lateral thigh is chosen because absorption there is faster than the arm, and subcutaneous absorption is too slow in anaphylaxis.

quiz.q: You are ramping a 350-pound patient for ventilation. The correct endpoint is:
choices: The patient sitting fully upright at 90 degrees
The shoulders elevated 6 inches above the head
The ear canal level with the sternal notch, head of the stretcher up 20-30 degrees
The head flat with padding under the occiput only
quiz.why: Ramping until the ear canal lines up with the sternal notch opens the airway axis and improves both the patient's own breathing and anyone's later attempt at the airway. Occipital padding alone flexes the neck in an obese patient, and full upright sitting makes bagging mechanically difficult.

quiz.q: Which statement about hyperoxia is correct?
choices: It reliably raises carbon dioxide in all patients
It improves coronary blood flow during a heart attack
It has no documented harms in the prehospital setting
It can cause absorption atelectasis by washing nitrogen out of alveoli
quiz.why: Nitrogen normally props alveoli open; wash it out with high oxygen concentrations and the alveoli collapse. Hyperoxia also produces free radicals and constricts coronary and cerebral vessels, which is the opposite of improving coronary flow. CO2 retention is a COPD-specific concern, not universal.

quiz.q: A term newborn requires resuscitation at delivery. Initial ventilation should begin with:
choices: Room air
40% oxygen by simple mask
CPAP at 10 cmH2O
100% oxygen
quiz.why: Term newborn resuscitation begins with room air, titrating oxygen up only if the saturation targets are not met. Starting at 100% exposes the newborn to oxidative injury with no survival benefit. CPAP is not the opening move in a newborn requiring resuscitation.

quiz.q: A diver surfaces rapidly and develops joint pain and shortness of breath. His SpO2 reads 98%. Oxygen management should be:
choices: Withhold oxygen since the saturation is normal
High-concentration oxygen regardless of the saturation
Nasal cannula at 2 L/min only
CPAP at 5 cmH2O
quiz.why: Decompression sickness is one of the situations where the number does not matter: high-concentration oxygen accelerates washout of nitrogen bubbles. Carbon monoxide poisoning and suspected cyanide are the other two. CPAP has no role here.

quiz.q: During adult CPR with no advanced airway, the pause to deliver two breaths should be:
choices: As long as needed for full chest rise on both breaths
Not required, because compressions provide ventilation
Under 10 seconds
About 20 seconds
quiz.why: Interruptions cost perfusion pressure, so the pause for two breaths stays under 10 seconds total. Taking longer to perfect the breaths trades a small ventilation gain for a large circulation loss. Compressions alone do provide some gas movement, but 30:2 remains the standard without an advanced airway.

quiz.q: Why is a post-ROSC patient placed with the head of the stretcher raised about 30 degrees when the blood pressure allows?
choices: To lower the ETCO2 toward 25 mmHg
To speed rewarming
To increase cerebral perfusion pressure directly
To reduce aspiration risk and support cerebral venous drainage
quiz.why: Head elevation helps drain cerebral venous blood and reduces aspiration in a patient who cannot protect the airway. It does not raise perfusion pressure, lowering ETCO2 is a harm rather than a goal, and aggressive rewarming is specifically avoided.

quiz.q: Before delivering the first breath in a cardiac arrest, suction should be:
choices: Turned on and within reach with a rigid tip attached
Set up only if the patient has a history of reflux
Requested from the responding paramedic unit
Left in the bag until vomiting occurs
quiz.why: Regurgitation during CPR is the expected complication, not an unusual one, so the rigid tip is running before the first breath. Setting up after vomiting starts costs you the airway and drives gastric contents into the lungs.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old having a panic attack is breathing 34 times a minute with clear lungs, an SpO2 of 100%, and tingling in the fingers. Her ETCO2 is 19 mmHg. The best explanation is:
choices: She is hypoxic and needs a nonrebreather
She is blowing off carbon dioxide faster than she produces it
She has a bronchospasm that the waveform cannot show
The sensor is off the patient
quiz.why: Rapid deep breathing with clear lungs and a saturation of 100% drops ETCO2 by exhaling CO2 faster than metabolism makes it, which causes the tingling. She is not hypoxic. Bronchospasm shows a shark-fin waveform, and a detached sensor produces no waveform at all.

quiz.q: An unresponsive adult with no trauma is breathing 16 times a minute with good chest rise and a strong pulse. There is a small amount of saliva in the mouth. The best positioning is:
choices: Prone with the head turned
Supine with an OPA in place
Recovery position on the side so secretions drain out
Fully upright in a chair
quiz.why: An unresponsive patient breathing adequately with no trauma belongs in the recovery position so gravity drains secretions away from the airway. An OPA may not be tolerated and does not protect against aspiration. Prone positioning impairs chest expansion and hides the airway from you.

quiz.q: A pocket mask with a one-way valve and oxygen at 15 L/min delivers roughly what concentration, and what is its practical advantage over one-rescuer bagging?
choices: About 21%, and it is faster to deploy
About 90%, and it prevents gastric distention entirely
Near 100%, and it requires no oxygen source
About 50-55%, and both of your hands can hold the seal
quiz.why: A pocket mask with supplemental oxygen at 15 L/min delivers roughly 50-55%, and because both hands hold the seal it often achieves better tidal volumes than a single rescuer squeezing a bag. It still requires oxygen, and no device prevents gastric distention entirely.
